questions.stem: A small lesion selectively damages the left medial lemniscus in the caudal medulla. Which modality is most directly affected on the contralateral side?

options.A: Pain and temperature from the face
options.B: Vibration and conscious proprioception from the body
options.C: Voluntary motor function of the tongue
options.E: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue

questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus contains second-order dorsal-column pathway fibres after they decussate as internal arcuate fibres in the caudal medulla. A lesion here therefore impairs contralateral vibration, discriminative touch and conscious proprioception from the body.

distractors.A: Facial pain and temperature are carried mainly by the spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus.
distractors.C: Tongue motor function is mediated by the hypoglossal nucleus and nerve (with supranuclear input).
distractors.D: Auditory pathways are bilateral above the cochlear nuclei; this is not the principal function of the medial lemniscus.
distractors.E: Taste from the anterior tongue travels through the chorda tympani to the solitary nucleus.

questions.correlation: A medial medullary syndrome may combine contralateral body weakness, contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception and ipsilateral tongue weakness, depending on structures involved.
questions.pearl: Remember: medial lemniscus = body discriminative touch, vibration and proprioception; spinal trigeminal system = facial pain and temperature.
references: Neuroanatomy teaching synthesis; verify against the current institutional curriculum before formal teaching.

questions.stem: In contemporary adult-type diffuse glioma classification, which statement best reflects the role of molecular markers?

options.A: Molecular markers are optional if the tumour has a typical MRI appearance
options.B: IDH status is a central defining feature in the classification of adult-type diffuse gliomas
options.C: All IDH-mutant gliomas are classified as glioblastoma
options.D: MGMT promoter methylation alone defines the integrated tumour type
options.E: Histology has been completely replaced by molecular testing

questions.explanation: Modern integrated diagnosis combines histological features with molecular findings. IDH status is central to distinguishing major adult-type diffuse glioma entities. The exact diagnostic work-up and terminology should follow the current WHO classification and local neuropathology practice.

distractors.A: MRI cannot establish an integrated molecular diagnosis; tissue and molecular work-up are usually required when clinically appropriate.
distractors.C: IDH-mutant astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma are distinct entities; IDH mutation does not by itself mean glioblastoma.
distractors.D: MGMT promoter methylation is clinically relevant, particularly as a predictive biomarker, but does not alone define the integrated tumour type.
distractors.E: Histology remains important and is integrated with molecular data.

questions.correlation: An integrated diagnosis influences prognostic discussion, multidisciplinary planning, trial eligibility and treatment pathways.
questions.pearl: Avoid using a radiological impression as a substitute for integrated histomolecular diagnosis.
references: WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Central Nervous System Tumours, 5th edition (2021); check for subsequent updates.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a sudden-onset, maximal-at-onset severe headache. Non-contrast CT is negative, but clinical suspicion for aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage remains. What is the safest general next principle?

options.A: Discharge because a negative CT excludes haemorrhage at any time point
options.B: Use a time- and pathway-appropriate further diagnostic strategy, guided by local protocol and specialist assessment
options.C: Start anticoagulation while awaiting outpatient imaging
options.D: Perform lumbar puncture in every patient without considering timing or contraindications
options.E: Assume migraine if the neurological examination is normal

questions.explanation: The sensitivity of non-contrast CT for subarachnoid blood depends on factors including time from onset, scanner quality and interpretation. If suspicion persists, further investigation may be required according to a validated local pathway, patient factors and specialist advice.

distractors.A: A negative CT does not universally exclude SAH; performance is time-dependent.
distractors.C: Empirical anticoagulation could be harmful if haemorrhage is present.
distractors.D: Lumbar puncture is not automatic for every patient; timing, contraindications and alternative imaging pathways matter.
distractors.E: A normal examination does not reliably exclude SAH.

questions.correlation: The diagnostic pathway affects subsequent decisions about vascular imaging, neurocritical care and aneurysm treatment.
questions.pearl: For thunderclap headache, document exact onset time and follow the locally approved SAH pathway; do not rely on a single negative test outside its validated context.
references: AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (2023); local pathway takes precedence.

questions.stem: Which new symptom in a patient with acute lumbar radicular pain should most strongly prompt urgent assessment for cauda equina syndrome?

options.C: New urinary retention or altered sensation of bladder filling
options.E: Chronic axial back pain without neurological change

questions.explanation: New urinary retention, altered bladder sensation, saddle sensory change and bowel/sexual dysfunction are important red flags for cauda equina syndrome. Clinical assessment and urgent imaging decisions should follow emergency pathways.

distractors.A: Cough-related exacerbation can occur with nerve-root irritation but is not by itself the most specific emergency red flag listed.
distractors.B: Unilateral sensory symptoms can occur with radiculopathy and require context, but are less concerning than new sphincter dysfunction.
distractors.D: Positional pain is common and is not the key red flag here.
distractors.E: Chronic stable axial pain without new neurological features is less suggestive of acute cauda equina syndrome.

questions.correlation: A focused history should ask about bladder sensation, ability to initiate micturition, saddle sensation, bowel function and sexual function.
questions.pearl: Do not use a single symptom or a normal digital rectal examination to rule out cauda equina syndrome; use the complete clinical picture and urgent local pathway.
references: NICE NG59, Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s; local emergency cauda equina pathway.

questions.stem: During the initial assessment of a patient with severe traumatic brain injury, which principle is most important?

options.A: Prioritise a detailed neurological examination before addressing airway and oxygenation
options.B: Prevent secondary brain injury by systematically addressing oxygenation, ventilation and circulation
options.C: Avoid cervical spine precautions once a head CT is requested
options.D: Treat hypotension as desirable to reduce cerebral blood flow
options.E: Delay treatment of extracranial haemorrhage until neurosurgical review

questions.explanation: Initial trauma care follows structured resuscitation principles. Hypoxia and hypotension can worsen secondary brain injury, so airway, oxygenation, ventilation and circulation require prompt attention alongside cervical spine protection and coordinated trauma care.

distractors.A: Life-threatening physiological problems take priority; the detailed neurological assessment follows stabilisation steps.
distractors.C: Cervical spine precautions remain relevant until cleared using an appropriate protocol.
distractors.D: Hypotension threatens cerebral perfusion and is not a therapeutic goal.
distractors.E: Life-threatening extracranial bleeding must be addressed promptly within the trauma team approach.

questions.correlation: Serial neurological observations, pupils, GCS components and physiological parameters help identify deterioration.
questions.pearl: Avoid preventable hypoxia and hypotension; document the GCS components rather than only a total score.
references: NICE NG232, Head injury: assessment and early management (2023); local trauma protocol.

questions.stem: Which finding in an infant may be a clinical clue to progressive hydrocephalus?

options.A: A stable head circumference tracking along its established percentile
options.B: A rapidly increasing head circumference crossing percentile lines
options.C: A single episode of uncomplicated hiccups
options.D: A normal, soft fontanelle during a calm examination

questions.explanation: A rapidly increasing head circumference, particularly when crossing centile lines, can indicate progressive ventricular enlargement in an infant. It must be interpreted with developmental history, examination and appropriate imaging.

distractors.A: A stable trajectory is generally less concerning than a rapid change, although it does not exclude disease.
distractors.C: Hiccups are non-specific and do not indicate hydrocephalus in isolation.
distractors.D: A soft fontanelle at one examination does not exclude hydrocephalus.
distractors.E: An isolated cough is not a characteristic indicator of progressive hydrocephalus.

questions.correlation: Assess head growth over time, fontanelle, sutures, eye movements, feeding, alertness and developmental progress.
questions.pearl: Trend measurements and interpret them in the child's clinical context; a single measurement is less informative.
references: Original educational synthesis; verify with current paediatric neurosurgery and local referral guidance.

questions.stem: After a penetrating injury, a learner examines a simulated patient with right leg spastic weakness and absent right toe position sense. Pinprick is reduced on the left beginning below T10. Where is the best single localization?
questions.explanation: The right hemicord contains already crossed corticospinal fibers and dorsal column fibers that have yet to cross. Pain fibers from the left cross within the cord and ascend on the right after a short segmental course.
questions.correlation: Partial hemicord injuries often yield an incomplete Brown-Séquard pattern.
questions.pearl: Localize the side from weakness and vibration loss before interpreting the pain level.

distractors.B: This would reverse the sides of weakness and proprioceptive loss.
distractors.C: This would impair position sense but would spare corticospinal and pain pathways.
distractors.D: A small central lesion preferentially interrupts crossing pain fibers bilaterally at the affected levels.
distractors.E: A plexus lesion causes lower motor neuron weakness and cannot explain left truncal sensory loss.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: A patient in a teaching vignette repeatedly misses objects approaching from either side. Formal perimetry shows loss of the temporal hemifield in both eyes with preserved nasal hemifields. Which site accounts for this pattern?
questions.explanation: Nasal retinal axons encode the temporal visual fields and cross in the optic chiasm. A midline chiasmal lesion can interrupt these axons from both eyes while sparing many uncrossed temporal retinal fibers.
questions.correlation: Suprasellar expansion from a sellar mass can compress the chiasm.
questions.pearl: Heteronymous temporal field loss points to the chiasm.

distractors.A: A complete lesion produces left monocular visual loss.
distractors.C: A lesion produces left homonymous field loss.
distractors.D: A lesion produces right homonymous loss, with extent depending on the fibers affected.
distractors.E: These relay hemifields from both eyes, rather than selectively relaying nasal retinal fibers.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: On attempted left gaze, the right eye fails to adduct and the left eye abducts with nystagmus. Right gaze is intact, and both eyes adduct with convergence. Which pathway is interrupted?
questions.explanation: The right medial longitudinal fasciculus carries internuclear signals from the left abducens nucleus to the right medial rectus subnucleus. Interruption impairs right adduction on left gaze while convergence can remain intact.
questions.correlation: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia localizes to the brainstem and can occur with demyelination or infarction.
questions.pearl: In internuclear ophthalmoplegia, name the affected side from the eye that fails to adduct.

distractors.A: This produces failed left adduction on right gaze.
distractors.B: The left eye would fail to abduct.
distractors.D: A medial rectus deficit from a nerve lesion also impairs adduction during convergence.
distractors.E: This impairs conjugate gaze to the right.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: In a teaching MRI, both lateral ventricles and the third ventricle are enlarged. The fourth ventricle is normal in size. Which single channel is most likely obstructed?
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct carries CSF from the third to the fourth ventricle. A blockage there expands the connected upstream ventricles while the fourth remains downstream.
questions.correlation: A lesion in the tectal region can narrow the aqueduct.
questions.pearl: Find the last enlarged ventricle and look at its outlet.

options.C: Median aperture of the fourth ventricle

distractors.A: An isolated right-sided blockage enlarges the right lateral ventricle upstream.
distractors.B: An isolated left-sided blockage enlarges the left lateral ventricle upstream.
distractors.C: This is downstream of the fourth ventricle and is one of several fourth ventricular outlets.
distractors.E: Impaired absorption usually produces communicating hydrocephalus with enlargement that includes the fourth ventricle.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: An adult develops acute right leg weakness and sensory loss, with much milder arm involvement and preserved facial movement. Imaging shows an infarct limited to the left medial hemisphere near the paracentral lobule. Which artery most directly supplies this area?
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies much of the medial frontal and parietal cortex. The paracentral lobule contains the leg representations of the primary motor and somatosensory cortices.
questions.correlation: An ACA territory lesion may also cause abulia when medial frontal circuits are involved.
questions.pearl: The leg lies on the medial surface of the sensorimotor homunculus.

distractors.A: It predominantly supplies lateral sensorimotor cortex, including face and arm representations.
distractors.B: Its typical cortical territory is occipital and inferomedial temporal.
distractors.C: It supplies deep structures including parts of the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
distractors.D: It supplies superior cerebellar territory, outside the medial cerebral hemisphere.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: After a midshaft humeral fracture, an adult cannot extend the wrist or the metacarpophalangeal joints and has decreased sensation in the dorsal first web space. Elbow extension is preserved. Which nerve is injured?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve runs along the humeral radial groove and supplies wrist and finger extensors as well as sensation in the first dorsal web space. Major triceps branches usually arise proximal to the groove.
questions.correlation: A lesion limited to the posterior interosseous nerve can weaken finger extension without cutaneous sensory loss.
questions.pearl: Dorsal first web space sensation tests a radial nerve territory.

distractors.B: A proximal injury affects thumb opposition and several wrist and finger flexors.
distractors.C: Typical weakness affects interossei and sensory loss involves the small finger.
distractors.D: It supplies elbow flexors and sensation over the lateral forearm.
distractors.E: It supplies deltoid and teres minor and sensation over the lateral shoulder.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: An adult has complete left facial weakness. Taste over the anterior tongue and sound tolerance are preserved. Imaging shows a lesion just after the facial nerve exits the skull. Through which opening did it exit?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve leaves its bony canal at the stylomastoid foramen. The chorda tympani and nerve to stapedius have usually already branched off, so an extracranial lesion can spare taste and stapedius function.
questions.correlation: A lesion of the facial nerve before it divides within the parotid can weaken the entire ipsilateral face.
questions.pearl: The facial nerve enters the temporal bone at the internal acoustic meatus and exits at the stylomastoid foramen.

distractors.A: CN IX, X and XI traverse it.
distractors.C: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve traverses it.
distractors.D: The hypoglossal nerve exits through it.
distractors.E: It carries orbital nerves including CN III, IV, V1 and VI.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: After an infarct limited to the dominant frontal cortex, a patient speaks in short, effortful phrases and cannot repeat a sentence. They follow simple commands and recognize pictured objects. Which cortical region best fits?
questions.explanation: The posterior inferior frontal gyrus is a component of the dominant language production network. Damage here can impair fluent expression and repetition, with relatively preserved comprehension for simple material.
questions.correlation: A persistent full Broca aphasia syndrome often involves tissue beyond the classic inferior frontal region.
questions.pearl: Assess fluency, comprehension and repetition separately.

distractors.A: Lesions there classically impair auditory language comprehension with fluent speech.
distractors.B: Injury causes visual field loss.
distractors.D: It primarily receives somatic sensory information.
distractors.E: Injury can reduce initiation, but does not best explain this language profile.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: A simulated patient with a small cerebellar lesion shows marked truncal sway and a broad-based gait. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing are near normal. Which region best explains the disproportionate axial deficit?
questions.explanation: The vermis integrates information about axial posture and contributes to control of trunk and proximal movements through medial cerebellar output. A midline lesion can cause severe truncal and gait ataxia with relatively preserved distal limb coordination.
questions.correlation: The pattern illustrates why gait and unsupported sitting can reveal dysfunction despite near-normal limb tests.
questions.pearl: Midline cerebellar dysfunction preferentially affects stance and gait.

distractors.A: This more often causes right appendicular dysmetria.
distractors.B: This more often causes left appendicular dysmetria.
distractors.C: Dentate dysfunction prominently affects planning and coordination of ipsilateral limb movement.
distractors.E: A focal lesion here would more strongly affect coordination on the left.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: A teaching CT shows a biconvex extra-axial blood collection deep to a fracture crossing the pterion. Which vessel is classically torn at this site?
questions.explanation: The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery runs against the inner skull near the pterion. A fracture can tear it and the accumulating blood separates dura from the skull.
questions.correlation: Epidural bleeding can also have a venous source, depending on the site of injury.
questions.pearl: Pterion fracture plus a lentiform extra-axial collection is the classic middle meningeal association.

distractors.A: Tearing typically produces subdural blood.
distractors.B: Rupture typically releases blood into the subarachnoid space.
distractors.C: Deep perforator rupture can produce intraparenchymal hemorrhage.
distractors.D: Bleeding from these enters the ventricular system.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: Where are the cell bodies of the first-order somatic sensory neurons supplying the trunk located?
questions.explanation: The sensory axon arises from a pseudounipolar neuron in a dorsal root ganglion. A peripheral branch reaches a receptor and a central branch enters the spinal cord through the dorsal root.
questions.correlation: A lesion distal to the ganglion can reduce peripheral sensory nerve action potentials.
questions.pearl: Dorsal roots carry sensory axons. Their cell bodies are in the dorsal root ganglion.

distractors.B: It contains lower motor neuron cell bodies.
distractors.C: It contains central neurons that receive or process sensory input.
distractors.D: It contains postganglionic sympathetic neurons.
distractors.E: It carries efferent axons and contains no sensory ganglion.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: Which artery accompanies the optic nerve through the optic canal in the usual anatomy?
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic artery typically arises from the internal carotid artery and enters the orbit through the optic canal with CN II. The superior orbital fissure is a separate passage.
questions.correlation: The optic canal is a confined space shared by the artery and nerve, an important relationship in skull-base anatomy.
questions.pearl: The optic canal transmits CN II and the ophthalmic artery.

distractors.A: It normally enters the cranium through the foramen spinosum.
distractors.C: It reaches the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure and then courses in the orbital floor.
distractors.D: It usually branches from the ophthalmic artery within the orbit.
distractors.E: It is a distal orbital branch that emerges near the medial supraorbital margin.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: A teaching case with a right dorsolateral medullary lesion shows hoarseness, dysphagia and reduced elevation of the right soft palate. Which nucleus best accounts for this cluster?
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus contains branchial motor neurons supplying pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles via the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. Its vagal component accounts for the combined palatal and laryngeal weakness.
questions.correlation: Lateral medullary lesions can produce severe swallowing and phonation deficits.
questions.pearl: Palatal weakness plus hoarseness suggests branchial motor involvement.

distractors.A: It controls tongue muscles.
distractors.B: It receives visceral sensory and taste input.
distractors.D: It processes facial pain and temperature.
distractors.E: Injury causes vertigo or imbalance rather than palatal paresis.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: After a left anterior temporal resection, automated perimetry shows a new right superior quadrantanopia in both eyes. Which fibers are most likely interrupted?
questions.explanation: Meyer’s loop carries fibers from inferior retina, representing the contralateral superior visual quadrant. The fibers sweep anteriorly into the temporal lobe before turning posteriorly toward the calcarine cortex.
questions.correlation: Temporal resections can encroach on the anterior optic radiation.
questions.pearl: Temporal optic radiation injury typically affects the opposite upper quadrant.

distractors.A: It carries information from the left superior visual quadrant.
distractors.B: It mainly carries the right inferior quadrant.
distractors.C: Its injury affects vision in the right eye only.
distractors.E: Its injury preferentially affects the temporal fields of both eyes.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: Following prolonged pressure against the lateral knee, a simulated patient has foot drop, weak eversion, and reduced sensation over most of the dorsum of the foot. Inversion and plantarflexion are strong. Which nerve best localizes the injury?
questions.explanation: The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck before dividing. Deep fibular involvement weakens dorsiflexion and superficial fibular involvement weakens eversion and sensation over much of the dorsum.
questions.correlation: Resisted inversion helps distinguish this pattern from an L5 root lesion because tibialis posterior uses the tibial nerve.
questions.pearl: Foot drop with weak eversion and strong inversion favors a common fibular lesion.

distractors.A: An isolated lesion usually spares eversion and limits sensory loss to the first web space.
distractors.B: An isolated lesion spares the ankle dorsiflexors.
distractors.C: Injury weakens plantarflexion and affects plantar sensation.
distractors.D: It is sensory and supplies the lateral foot rather than the dorsiflexors.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: In a teaching case, a patient eats from the right side of a plate and omits the left side of a scene when drawing. They detect targets in either hemifield when presented singly but miss the left target during bilateral stimulation. Which region best explains the deficit?
questions.explanation: The right temporoparietal region participates in attention networks that distribute salience across space. A lesion can impair attention to left stimuli, especially when a competing right stimulus is present.
questions.correlation: Extinction on double simultaneous stimulation can expose an attentional deficit when testing one stimulus at a time appears normal.
questions.pearl: Extinction during competition helps distinguish neglect from a fixed field cut.

distractors.B: A lesion causes right homonymous field loss.
distractors.C: A lesion can impair detection of isolated left-field visual stimuli.
distractors.D: In the dominant hemisphere, injury commonly affects speech production.
distractors.E: An isolated lesion produces left hand weakness rather than spatial extinction.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: Which vessel directly connects the left and right anterior cerebral arteries at the front of the arterial circle?
questions.explanation: The anterior communicating artery bridges the proximal anterior cerebral arteries at the junction of their A1 and A2 segments. It completes the anterior part of the circle and can convey collateral flow between sides.
questions.correlation: The anterior communicating complex is a common location for intracranial aneurysms.
questions.pearl: Anterior communicating is a cross-midline bridge. Posterior communicating is an ipsilateral carotid-to-posterior-cerebral connection.

distractors.A: It connects the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery on the same side.
distractors.C: It supplies deep structures and does not bridge the ACAs.
distractors.D: It is an ACA perforating branch that supplies deep anterior structures.
distractors.E: It forms from the vertebral arteries and ends at the posterior cerebral arteries.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: Which named opening directly connects each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle?
questions.explanation: The paired interventricular foramina are the passages from the lateral ventricles into the midline third ventricle. The aqueduct begins farther downstream at the posterior third ventricle.
questions.correlation: A colloid cyst near the anterior third ventricle can obstruct flow at one or both foramina.
questions.pearl: Monro is upstream of the third ventricle. The aqueduct is downstream.

distractors.A: It connects the fourth ventricle to the subarachnoid space.
distractors.B: It is a paired exit from the fourth ventricle.
distractors.D: It connects the third and fourth ventricles.
distractors.E: It is at the caudal apex of the fourth ventricle near the central canal.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: Which cell type provides the output of the cerebellar cortex to its deep nuclei?
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells integrate inputs from parallel and climbing fibers. Their axons carry inhibitory GABAergic output from the cerebellar cortex to deep nuclei, with some projections also reaching vestibular nuclei.
questions.correlation: Loss of Purkinje cells disrupts the timing and modulation of cerebellar output.
questions.pearl: Cerebellar cortex sends inhibitory output through Purkinje axons.

distractors.A: Their parallel fibers excite Purkinje cells within the cortex.
distractors.B: They are local inhibitory interneurons that target Purkinje cells.
distractors.C: They regulate granule cells in the granular layer.
distractors.E: They send climbing fiber input into the cortex.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: Between which two meningeal layers is CSF normally found around the cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explanation: The arachnoid bridges over the sulci while the pia follows the brain surface. The subarachnoid space between them contains CSF, trabeculae and vessels.
questions.correlation: Blood in this space can track into cortical sulci and basal cisterns.
questions.pearl: Pia follows the sulci. Arachnoid bridges them.

distractors.A: The subdural compartment is a potential cleavage plane rather than the normal CSF space.
distractors.B: This is the potential cranial epidural plane.
distractors.C: Separation of dural layers forms venous sinuses in specific locations.
distractors.D: Pia covers the cortical surface, deep to the subarachnoid space.

references: Greenberg’s Handbook of Neurosurgery (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)
Khalid and Citow, Neurosurgery Primary Examination Review (Thieme; curriculum bibliography)

questions.stem: Which layer closely follows the surface of the brain down into its grooves?
questions.explanation: The pia adheres to the contours of the brain, so it dips into the sulci.

distractors.A: The arachnoid generally bridges the sulci.
distractors.B: This layer forms dural folds away from the contours of individual gyri.
distractors.D: This outer dural layer lines the inside of the skull.
distractors.E: Ependyma lines the ventricles, away from the external surface.

references: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § I Meninges, pp. 2–3

questions.stem: Why can the cisterna magna hold more CSF locally than the space over a closely apposed brain surface?

options.A: Arachnoid and pia are farther apart there.
options.B: The skull separates from the dura there.
options.C: The two dural layers enclose CSF there.
options.D: The arachnoid reaches deepest into every nearby sulcus.
options.E: CSF is secreted into the tissue below the pia.

questions.explanation: A cistern is a local widening of the subarachnoid space. The membranes remain the same.

distractors.B: That would create an epidural space rather than enlarge a cistern.
distractors.C: Separation of dural layers can form a venous sinus, which carries blood.
distractors.D: The pia follows the grooves. Cistern size depends on the gap between the layers.
distractors.E: Most CSF comes from choroid plexuses within ventricles and then flows into cisterns.

references: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § I Meninges, pp. 2–3

questions.stem: On a teaching CT, fresh blood traces several cortical sulci without forming a single smooth collection. Which compartment best explains the distribution?
questions.explanation: This space follows the grooves around surface vessels. Blood within it can trace their branching pattern.

distractors.A: An epidural collection lies outside the dura and is typically shaped by its skull attachments.
distractors.B: A subdural collection can drape over the hemisphere as a crescent without tracking each sulcus.
distractors.C: Ventricular blood outlines an internal cavity rather than cortical grooves.
distractors.E: A sinus is a bounded venous channel within the dura.

references: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § I Meninges, pp. 2–3

questions.stem: A teaching scan shows an extra-axial collection crossing a calvarial suture but stopping at the falx. Which anatomical explanation best fits both boundaries?

options.A: The collection dissects between skull and dura.
options.B: The collection spreads deep to the dura and is limited by its fold.
options.C: The collection flows in the ventricular system.
options.D: The collection is confined to a cortical artery.
options.E: The collection expands the diploic space.

questions.explanation: A subdural collection lies inside the skull attachment plane. It can cross sutures while dural reflections limit its spread.

distractors.A: This is the epidural plane, where dural attachment at sutures commonly limits extension.
distractors.C: Ventricular shape follows internal cavities and their connections.
distractors.D: The vessel wall would define its boundary.
distractors.E: The diploë lies within cranial bone and is outside the meningeal folds.

distractors.A: Hippocampal formation. This medial temporal system is important for forming new declarative memories. The role asked about here belongs to Entorhinal cortex.
distractors.B: Dentate gyrus. This component contains granule cells and participates in hippocampal input circuitry. The role asked about here belongs to Entorhinal cortex.
distractors.D: Fornix. The fornix carries major hippocampal outputs toward septal and hypothalamic targets. The role asked about here belongs to Entorhinal cortex.
distractors.E: Amygdala. This nearby medial temporal structure contributes to emotional significance and emotional learning. The role asked about here belongs to Entorhinal cortex.

questions.learning_objective: Explain the anatomical role of Entorhinal cortex.
references: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XI Hippocampal Formation, pp. 55–58

questions.stem: What is the tapered lower end of the adult spinal cord called?
questions.explanation: Conus medullaris. The conus is the tapered lower end of the adult cord, usually near vertebral levels L1–L2.

distractors.A: Cauda equina. This bundle contains descending lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerve roots below the cord. The role asked about here belongs to Conus medullaris.
distractors.C: Dorsal columns. These pathways carry vibration, discriminative touch and conscious position sense toward the medulla. The role asked about here belongs to Conus medullaris.
distractors.D: Anterolateral system. This system carries pain and temperature; many fibers cross near their spinal entry level after synapsing. The role asked about here belongs to Conus medullaris.
distractors.E: Ventral horn. This region contains lower motor neuron cell bodies whose axons supply skeletal muscles. The role asked about here belongs to Conus medullaris.

topics.title: Medial medullary anatomy
topics.summary: A concise review of the medial medulla, long tracts and clinical localisation.

sections.heading: Key structures
sections.body: The medial medulla contains the pyramid (corticospinal fibres), medial lemniscus (crossed dorsal-column pathway fibres) and hypoglossal nucleus/fascicles.

sections.heading: Clinical localisation
sections.body: A lesion may produce contralateral weakness, contralateral impairment of vibration/proprioception and ipsilateral tongue weakness. The exact pattern depends on lesion extent.

sections.heading: Exam focus
sections.body: Localise each deficit to a tract or nucleus before naming a syndrome. Distinguish body sensory pathways from facial sensory pathways.

topics.title: Integrated diagnosis in diffuse glioma
topics.summary: Why modern glioma diagnosis combines morphology and molecular markers.

sections.heading: Integrated approach
sections.body: Diagnosis combines clinical context, imaging, histopathology and molecular findings. IDH status is central to adult-type diffuse glioma classification.

sections.heading: Biomarkers
sections.body: MGMT promoter methylation can inform treatment discussions in relevant settings but does not alone define the integrated tumour entity.

sections.heading: Clinical application
sections.body: Use the final neuropathology report and current multidisciplinary guidance rather than inferring tumour type from imaging alone.

topics.title: Cauda equina red flags
topics.summary: A structured history for possible cauda equina syndrome.

sections.heading: Ask directly
sections.body: Clarify urinary sensation, initiation, stream, retention/incontinence, saddle sensation, bowel function and sexual function.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.body: No single symptom or bedside finding safely excludes cauda equina syndrome. Use the full clinical picture and urgent local pathway.

sections.heading: Documentation
sections.body: Record onset and progression, bilateral symptoms, motor findings, sensory distribution, sphincter symptoms and escalation decisions.

flashcards.front: Which sensory modalities travel in the medial lemniscus?
flashcards.back: Vibration, discriminative touch and conscious proprioception from the contralateral body after decussation in the caudal medulla.

flashcards.front: What does an integrated glioma diagnosis combine?
flashcards.back: Histological morphology with relevant molecular findings, interpreted under the current WHO classification.

flashcards.front: Name key bladder-related red flags in possible cauda equina syndrome.
flashcards.back: New urinary retention, altered bladder-filling sensation, difficulty initiating micturition and new incontinence; assess alongside saddle, bowel and sexual symptoms.

flashcards.front: Which two physiological threats are especially important to prevent in severe TBI?
flashcards.back: Hypoxia and hypotension, as contributors to secondary brain injury.

sections.heading: Meninges
sections.title: Meninges
sections.objective: Identify the three layers and locate blood or CSF relative to them.
sections.planned_objective: Trace meningeal vessels and sensory innervation and compare cisterns with perivascular spaces.
notes: From skull to brain the order is dura, arachnoid and pia. The dura is tough and forms partitions such as the falx and tentorium. The arachnoid bridges grooves, while the pia follows the brain surface into them. CSF and major surface vessels lie between arachnoid and pia. Where the membranes are farther apart, this space widens into a cistern.

Think about what bounds a collection. Intracranial epidural blood separates dura from skull and is often limited by sutures. Subdural blood spreads near the dura–arachnoid interface and can extend across sutures but is constrained by dural folds. Blood in the subarachnoid space can follow sulci and cisterns.

Dura mater. The dura is the tough outer covering and forms the falx and tentorium. Arachnoid mater. The arachnoid bridges sulci and bounds the subarachnoid space externally. Pia mater. The pia follows the brain surface and contributes to the denticulate ligaments of the cord. Subarachnoid space. This space between arachnoid and pia contains CSF and surface vessels. Dural venous sinus. A dural sinus is a venous blood channel between dural layers.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § I Meninges, pp. 2–3

sections.heading: Cerebrospinal Fluid
sections.title: Cerebrospinal Fluid
sections.objective: Trace ventricular flow and predict which cavities enlarge above an obstruction.
sections.planned_objective: Compare CSF composition, clearance routes, cisterns and pressure–volume relationships.
notes: Most CSF is secreted by the choroid plexuses. From each lateral ventricle it passes through an interventricular foramen into the third ventricle, then through the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth. A median and two lateral apertures lead to the subarachnoid space. CSF provides buoyancy and helps maintain a stable fluid environment.

Draw arrows before considering ventricular size. With an isolated block, cavities upstream can expand while those downstream may remain unchanged. If flow through the ventricles is open but clearance outside them is impaired, the fourth ventricle can enlarge too. Arachnoid granulations and lymphatic pathways contribute to clearance.

Choroid plexus. The choroid plexus secretes most CSF into the ventricles. Interventricular foramen. This opening connects a lateral ventricle to the third ventricle. Cerebral aqueduct. The aqueduct links the third and fourth ventricles through the midbrain. Fourth-ventricle apertures. The median and lateral apertures let CSF enter the subarachnoid space. Arachnoid granulations. Granulations contribute to CSF clearance into dural venous sinuses.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § II Cerebrospinal Fluid, pp. 3–6

sections.heading: Brain Barriers
sections.title: Brain Barriers
sections.objective: Distinguish the blood–brain and blood–CSF interfaces by cell type and compartment.
sections.planned_objective: Compare transport routes, regional permeability and specialized ventricular interfaces.
notes: Follow a molecule from blood into brain tissue. At most brain capillaries, tight junctions between endothelial cells limit passage between cells. Pericytes and astrocyte endfeet help support the barrier. Some substances diffuse through cells, while others such as glucose use transport proteins.

At the choroid plexus, capillaries let many solutes enter the underlying tissue. Tight junctions between epithelial cells control the next step into ventricular CSF. Some areas, such as the area postrema, have specialized permeable capillaries and can sample circulating signals.

Brain capillary endothelial cells. Their tight junctions form the principal seal of the blood–brain barrier. Choroid plexus epithelial cells. Their tight junctions form the blood–CSF barrier at the plexus. Astrocyte endfeet. These processes surround brain vessels from the tissue side and support barrier properties. Glucose transport proteins. These proteins carry glucose across cell membranes at the blood–brain barrier. Circumventricular organs. These specialized regions include sites with permeable capillaries that detect blood-borne signals.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § III Brain Barriers, pp. 6–8

sections.heading: Blood Supply to the Brain
sections.title: Blood Supply to the Brain
sections.objective: Predict basic deficits from medial, lateral and occipital cortical territories.
sections.planned_objective: Follow great vessels, choroidal and perforating branches, collaterals, regional perfusion and venous drainage.
notes: Start with two arterial systems. The internal carotids feed most of the anterior circulation. Vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery. The communicating arteries link the circulations at the base of the brain. ACA territory includes medial frontal leg areas, MCA territory covers much of the lateral cortex, and PCA territory includes visual cortex. Compare these surface territories with deep perforators that supply compact pathways such as the internal capsule.

Anterior cerebral artery. The ACA supplies much of the medial hemisphere, including the cortical leg area. Middle cerebral artery. The MCA supplies much of the lateral cortex, including face-arm motor areas and major language regions. Posterior cerebral artery. The PCA supplies much of the occipital lobe, including primary visual cortex. Basilar artery. The vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery along the ventral pons. Anterior communicating artery. This artery connects the right and left anterior cerebral arteries.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § IV Blood Supply to the Brain, pp. 8–27

sections.heading: Blood Supply to the Spinal Cord
sections.title: Blood Supply to the Spinal Cord
sections.objective: Draw the anterior and posterior spinal arterial territories.
sections.planned_objective: Identify segmental reinforcement, sulcal branches, venous routes and regional vulnerability.
notes: Longitudinal spinal arteries receive reinforcement from segmental vessels. The anterior spinal artery supplies much of the anterior cord, including motor and anterolateral pathways. Paired posterior spinal arteries supply much of the dorsal cord. This arrangement helps explain how motor and pain-temperature function can be impaired while position sense is relatively preserved.

Anterior spinal artery. This midline artery supplies much of the anterior two-thirds of the cord. Posterior spinal arteries. These paired longitudinal arteries supply much of the dorsal cord, including dorsal columns. Segmental medullary arteries. These vessels reinforce the longitudinal spinal arteries at different levels. Artery of Adamkiewicz. This large anterior segmental medullary artery reinforces anterior blood supply to the lower cord. Spinal veins. These veins drain blood away from the spinal cord toward venous plexuses.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § V Blood Supply to the Spinal Cord, pp. 28–30

sections.heading: Cortical Anatomy
sections.title: Cortical Anatomy
sections.objective: Locate primary motor, sensory and visual cortices using nearby sulci.
sections.planned_objective: Compare cortical layers, functional areas, motor inputs, dominance and association networks.
notes: Use the central sulcus as a boundary. Voluntary motor output is strongly associated with the gyrus just in front of it, and primary body sensation with the gyrus just behind it. The calcarine sulcus anchors the map of the visual field. Language requires distributed networks, typically with left-hemisphere dominance.

Precentral gyrus. This gyrus lies in front of the central sulcus and contains primary motor cortex. Postcentral gyrus. This gyrus lies behind the central sulcus and contains primary somatosensory cortex. Calcarine cortex. The banks of the calcarine sulcus contain primary visual cortex. Dominant inferior frontal gyrus. Its posterior portion includes important components of the speech production network. Insula. This cortex lies deep in the lateral sulcus beneath the opercula.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § VI Cortical Anatomy, pp. 30–39

sections.heading: Diencephalon
sections.title: Diencephalon
sections.objective: Distinguish a thalamic relay from fibers passing through the internal capsule.
sections.planned_objective: Map thalamic nuclei, epithalamus, capsule subdivisions and their blood supply.
notes: The thalamus processes and relays information within circuits linking cortex and subcortical structures. Body and face sensation use different thalamic relays. The neighboring internal capsule is packed with ascending and descending fibers. A small lesion there can affect several body regions because the fibers run close together.

Ventral posterolateral nucleus. The VPL relays somatic sensation from the body toward cortex. Ventral posteromedial nucleus. The VPM relays somatic sensation from the face toward cortex. Lateral geniculate nucleus. This thalamic relay carries visual information toward visual cortex. Medial geniculate nucleus. This thalamic relay carries auditory information toward auditory cortex. Internal capsule. This compact white-matter region beside the thalamus carries many ascending and descending fibers.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § VII Diencephalon, pp. 40–46

sections.heading: Basal Ganglia
sections.title: Basal Ganglia
sections.objective: Explain how inhibitory output can regulate movement selection.
sections.planned_objective: Map the main nuclei, fiber landmarks, vascular supply and direct, indirect and hyperdirect pathways.
notes: The caudate and putamen form the dorsal striatum, a major entry point for cortical signals. Output from the internal pallidum and substantia nigra pars reticulata normally restrains targets such as the thalamus. In the simplified direct pathway, inhibiting that output reduces the restraint on the thalamus. This is disinhibition.

Dorsal striatum. Caudate and putamen form the dorsal striatum, a major input region of basal ganglia circuits. Lentiform nucleus. This anatomical grouping consists of putamen and globus pallidus. Substantia nigra pars compacta. This midbrain region supplies dopaminergic input to the striatum. Globus pallidus internus. The internal pallidal segment is a major source of inhibitory basal ganglia output. Subthalamic nucleus. This nucleus excites basal ganglia output nuclei and participates in movement suppression.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § VIII Basal Ganglia, pp. 46–51

sections.heading: Hypothalamus
sections.title: Hypothalamus
sections.objective: Contrast hypothalamic communication with the anterior and posterior pituitary.
sections.planned_objective: Relate hypothalamic nuclei to homeostasis, autonomic output and hypophyseal blood supply.
notes: The hypothalamus integrates signals about the body's internal state. Releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary through portal vessels. Vasopressin and oxytocin travel along hypothalamic axons to the posterior pituitary, where they can enter the circulation.

Suprachiasmatic nucleus. This nucleus receives retinal input and helps synchronize daily rhythms. Supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei. Neurons in these nuclei synthesize vasopressin and oxytocin. Hypophyseal portal vessels. These vessels carry hypothalamic releasing hormones to the anterior pituitary. Posterior pituitary. This neural extension stores and releases hormones delivered along hypothalamic axons. Mammillary bodies. These hypothalamic structures participate in memory circuits and connect with anterior thalamic nuclei.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § IX Hypothalamus, pp. 51–54

sections.heading: Olfactory System
sections.title: Olfactory System
sections.objective: Trace a signal from the olfactory epithelium to primary olfactory cortex.
sections.planned_objective: Compare the olfactory striae and bulb outputs and relate smell to memory and perception.
notes: Olfactory receptor axons pass through the cribriform plate to reach the bulb. Bulb output travels in the olfactory tract to primary olfactory regions including piriform cortex. The signal can reach primary olfactory cortex before a thalamic relay. Higher processing can still involve the thalamus.

Olfactory receptor neurons. These neurons in the nasal olfactory epithelium detect odor molecules. Cribriform plate. Small olfactory nerve bundles cross openings in this part of the ethmoid bone. Olfactory bulb. Olfactory receptor axons synapse in the bulb, including onto mitral and tufted cells. Olfactory tract. This tract carries output from the bulb toward primary olfactory regions. Piriform cortex. This primary olfactory cortex receives input without an obligatory preceding thalamic relay.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § X Olfactory System, pp. 54–55

sections.heading: Hippocampal Formation
sections.title: Hippocampal Formation
sections.objective: Connect hippocampal anatomy to formation of new declarative memories.
sections.planned_objective: Trace intrinsic circuitry, fornix outputs and limbic connections including the Papez circuit.
notes: The hippocampal formation lies in the medial temporal lobe. Entorhinal cortex is a major route for cortical input. Dentate gyrus, hippocampus and subiculum form a connected sequence, and the fornix is a major output route. Bilateral injury can interfere markedly with forming new explicit memories.

Hippocampal formation. This medial temporal system is important for forming new declarative memories. Entorhinal cortex. This cortex is a major interface between the hippocampal formation and other cortical areas. Dentate gyrus. This component contains granule cells and participates in hippocampal input circuitry. Fornix. The fornix carries major hippocampal outputs toward septal and hypothalamic targets. Amygdala. This nearby medial temporal structure contributes to emotional significance and emotional learning.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XI Hippocampal Formation, pp. 55–58

sections.heading: Cerebellum
sections.title: Cerebellum
sections.objective: Relate midline and hemispheric regions to different coordination tasks.
sections.planned_objective: Trace peduncles, spinocerebellar pathways, cortical inputs, Purkinje output and deep nuclei.
notes: The cerebellum helps adjust timing and accuracy. Midline structures contribute to control of posture and gait, while intermediate and lateral regions contribute to limb control and planning. Purkinje cells are the output neurons of cerebellar cortex and inhibit their targets, including the deep nuclei.

Vermis. The midline vermis is especially involved in axial control, posture and gait. Lateral cerebellar hemisphere. This region contributes to planning and coordinating skilled limb movements. Purkinje cells. These cerebellar cortical output neurons inhibit their targets. Middle cerebellar peduncle. This peduncle carries a large input from pontine nuclei into the cerebellum. Flocculonodular lobe. This region has close vestibular connections and contributes to balance and eye movement control.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XII Cerebellum, pp. 59–65

sections.heading: Cranial Nerves
sections.title: Cranial Nerves
sections.objective: Relate key nerve functions to eye movements, facial sensation and facial movement.
sections.planned_objective: Trace each nerve I–XII from its origin or nucleus to exit, targets and representative lesion patterns.
notes: Start with one action per nerve. VI abducts the eye through lateral rectus. IV supplies superior oblique, which helps depress the adducted eye. III supplies most remaining eye movements, eyelid elevation and pupillary constriction. V carries most facial sensation and drives mastication. VII drives facial expression and also carries taste and autonomic fibers.

Optic nerve, CN II. The optic nerve carries visual information from the retina toward the brain. Oculomotor nerve, CN III. CN III supplies most extraocular muscles, levator palpebrae and parasympathetic fibers for pupil constriction. Trigeminal nerve, CN V. CN V carries most facial sensation; its mandibular division supplies chewing muscles. Facial nerve, CN VII. CN VII supplies facial expression and carries taste and parasympathetic fibers. Hypoglossal nerve, CN XII. CN XII supplies most tongue muscles and is important for tongue movement.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XIII Cranial Nerves, pp. 65–79

sections.heading: Brainstem
sections.title: Brainstem
sections.objective: Use a cranial nerve sign with a long-tract sign to orient to level and side.
sections.planned_objective: Compare midbrain, pontine and medullary cross-sections, nuclei, tract crossings and vascular territories.
notes: Read the brainstem from top to bottom as midbrain, pons and medulla. A cranial nerve finding can anchor the level. Long pathways often carry signals from the opposite body side at the lesion level. For example, involvement of a hypoglossal fascicle and a pyramid above its crossing can affect the tongue on one side and the limbs on the other.

Midbrain. The upper brainstem contains the colliculi and nuclei associated with CN III and IV. Pons. The pons lies between midbrain and medulla and contains major relays to the cerebellum. Medulla oblongata. The lowest brainstem region contains the pyramids and nuclei for several lower cranial nerves. Superior colliculus. This midbrain structure helps orient eyes and head toward visual stimuli. Inferior colliculus. This midbrain structure is an important relay for auditory processing.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XIV Brainstem, pp. 79–89

sections.heading: Spine and Spinal Cord
sections.title: Spine and Spinal Cord
sections.objective: Compare spinal levels, roots and the crossing points of major tracts.
sections.planned_objective: Map gray matter laminae, segmental structures, ligaments, joints and canal anatomy.
notes: Vertebral level and spinal cord segment diverge because the spine grows farther caudally. Lumbar and sacral roots continue below the conus as the cauda equina. In the cord, dorsal columns carry vibration and position sense toward a crossing in the medulla. Pain and temperature fibers generally cross near their spinal entry level after synapsing.

Conus medullaris. The conus is the tapered lower end of the adult cord, usually near vertebral levels L1–L2. Cauda equina. This bundle contains descending lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerve roots below the cord. Dorsal columns. These pathways carry vibration, discriminative touch and conscious position sense toward the medulla. Anterolateral system. This system carries pain and temperature; many fibers cross near their spinal entry level after synapsing. Ventral horn. This region contains lower motor neuron cell bodies whose axons supply skeletal muscles.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XV Spine and Spinal Cord, pp. 89–99

sections.heading: Cranial Foramina and Miscellaneous Structures
sections.title: Cranial Foramina and Miscellaneous Structures
sections.objective: Predict which trigeminal division passes through key skull-base openings.
sections.planned_objective: Map other foraminal contents, bony landmarks, craniometric points and cavernous sinus triangles.
notes: The ophthalmic division enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. The maxillary division leaves the middle cranial fossa through foramen rotundum, and the mandibular division through foramen ovale. Group structures by destination to make skull-base routes easier to reconstruct.

Foramen rotundum. The maxillary trigeminal division, V2, passes through foramen rotundum. Foramen ovale. The mandibular trigeminal division, V3, passes through foramen ovale. Foramen spinosum. The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through foramen spinosum. Jugular foramen. CN IX, X and XI pass through this opening beside important venous structures. Hypoglossal canal. CN XII passes through this canal in the occipital bone.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XVI Cranial Foramina and Miscellaneous Structures, pp. 99–104

sections.heading: Orbit and Tendinous Ring (Anulus of Zinn)
sections.title: Orbit and Tendinous Ring (Anulus of Zinn)
sections.objective: Distinguish passage through the optic canal from passage through the superior orbital fissure.
sections.planned_objective: Map the relationship of orbital nerves and vessels to the ring and extraocular muscle origins.
notes: The common tendinous ring anchors the four rectus muscles at the orbital apex. The optic nerve and ophthalmic artery enter through the optic canal. Oculomotor divisions, nasociliary nerve and abducens pass through the part of the superior orbital fissure inside the ring. The trochlear nerve passes outside the ring.

Optic canal. The optic nerve and ophthalmic artery enter the orbit through this canal. Superior orbital fissure. CN III, IV, VI and branches of V1 enter the orbit through this fissure. Common tendinous ring. This ring at the orbital apex anchors the four rectus muscles. Trochlear nerve. CN IV supplies superior oblique and enters through the superior orbital fissure outside the ring. Abducens nerve. CN VI supplies lateral rectus and passes through the superior orbital fissure inside the ring.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XVII Orbit and Tendinous Ring (Anulus of Zinn), pp. 104–105

sections.heading: Innervation and Muscles of the Head and Neck
sections.title: Innervation and Muscles of the Head and Neck
sections.objective: Associate mastication, expression and shoulder elevation with motor nerves.
sections.planned_objective: Compare orbital, branchial, cervical, tongue and swallowing muscle groups and their innervation.
notes: Link muscle groups by function. The mandibular division of V drives the major chewing muscles. VII supplies muscles of facial expression. XI supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Most intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles receive XII, with palatoglossus supplied through the vagal pharyngeal plexus.

Mandibular division of V. V3 supplies major chewing muscles, including masseter and temporalis. Facial nerve. CN VII supplies facial expression and the stapedius muscle. Accessory nerve. CN XI supplies the main motor input to sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Hypoglossal nerve. CN XII supplies most tongue muscles; palatoglossus receives its motor supply through the vagal pharyngeal plexus. Vagus nerve. CN X supplies most palatal and pharyngeal muscles via the pharyngeal plexus and supplies the larynx through its branches.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XVIII Innervation and Muscles of the Head and Neck, pp. 105–106

sections.heading: Peripheral Nerve Plexi
sections.title: Peripheral Nerve Plexi
sections.objective: Distinguish a root pattern from a terminal nerve pattern.
sections.planned_objective: Trace cervical, brachial, lumbar and sacral plexuses from ventral rami to representative branches.
notes: Plexuses redistribute fibers from spinal ventral rami into peripheral nerves. In the brachial plexus, roots combine into trunks, split into divisions and regroup into cords before major terminal branches. A root lesion can affect muscles belonging to several different terminal nerves.

Phrenic nerve. The phrenic nerve receives C3–C5 fibers and supplies the diaphragm. Brachial plexus. This plexus usually arises from ventral rami C5–T1 and supplies the upper limb. Lumbar plexus. This plexus, mainly L1–L4, gives rise to major nerves including femoral and obturator nerves. Sacral plexus. This plexus, usually L4–S4, contributes to nerves including the sciatic nerve. Ansa cervicalis. This cervical loop, mainly C1–C3, supplies several infrahyoid strap muscles.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XIX Peripheral Nerve Plexi, pp. 106–110

sections.heading: Structures to Memorize
sections.title: Structures to Memorize
sections.objective: Recall structure, endpoints and function together.
sections.planned_objective: Build recall sets for fascicles, commissures, nuclei, ganglia, autonomic pathways and sensory nerves.
notes: Use three prompts for each structure. Where does it start, where does it go, and what does it carry? For example, the medial longitudinal fasciculus links relevant brainstem nuclei to coordinate eye movements. Use a second pass to contrast similarly named structures, such as sensory ganglia and autonomic ganglia.

Corpus callosum. This large commissure connects many cortical areas of the two cerebral hemispheres. Medial longitudinal fasciculus. The MLF links relevant vestibular and ocular motor nuclei to coordinate eye movements. Medial lemniscus. This ascending pathway carries dorsal-column information onward from medulla toward thalamus. Lateral lemniscus. This pathway participates in auditory transmission through the brainstem. Mammillothalamic tract. This tract links mammillary bodies to anterior thalamic nuclei in a memory circuit.
sections.reading: Citow et al., Comprehensive Neurosurgery Board Review, 3rd ed. (Thieme, 2020), ch. 1, § XX Structures to Memorize, pp. 111–112

questions.stem: Eine kleine Läsion schädigt selektiv den linken Lemniscus medialis in der kaudalen Medulla oblongata. Welche Modalität ist auf der kontralateralen Seite am stärksten beeinträchtigt?

options.B: Vibrationsempfinden und bewusste Propriozeption des Körpers
options.E: Geschmack der vorderen zwei Drittel der Zunge

questions.explanation: Der Lemniscus medialis enthält Fasern des Hinterstrangsystems nach ihrer Kreuzung als Fibrae arcuatae internae in der kaudalen Medulla oblongata. Eine Läsion an dieser Stelle beeinträchtigt daher kontralateral Vibrationsempfinden, diskriminierende Berührung und bewusste Propriozeption des Körpers.

distractors.A: Schmerz und Temperatur aus dem Gesicht werden überwiegend über den Tractus und Nucleus spinalis nervi trigemini geleitet.
distractors.C: Die Zungenmotorik wird durch den Nucleus und Nervus hypoglossus sowie supranukleäre Bahnen vermittelt.
distractors.D: Die Hörbahn ist oberhalb der Cochleariskerne bilateral verschaltet; der Lemniscus medialis ist nicht primär für das Hören zuständig.
distractors.E: Geschmacksfasern der vorderen Zunge ziehen über die Chorda tympani zum Nucleus tractus solitarii.

questions.correlation: Ein mediales Medullasyndrom kann – abhängig von der Ausdehnung – kontralaterale Körperparese, kontralateralen Verlust von Vibration/Propriozeption und ipsilaterale Zungenschwäche kombinieren.
questions.pearl: Merke: Lemniscus medialis = diskriminierende Sensibilität, Vibration und Propriozeption des Körpers; spinales Trigeminussystem = Schmerz und Temperatur im Gesicht.
references: Neuroanatomische Lehrzusammenfassung; vor einer formalen Lehreinheit mit dem aktuellen institutionellen Curriculum abgleichen.

questions.stem: Welche Aussage beschreibt die Rolle molekularer Marker in der aktuellen Klassifikation adulter diffuser Gliome am besten?

options.A: Molekulare Marker sind entbehrlich, wenn das MRT-Bild typisch ist
options.B: Der IDH-Status ist ein zentrales definierendes Merkmal bei der Klassifikation adulter diffuser Gliome
options.C: Alle IDH-mutierten Gliome werden als Glioblastom klassifiziert
options.D: Eine MGMT-Promotor-Methylierung allein definiert den integrierten Tumortyp
options.E: Die Histologie wurde vollständig durch molekulare Tests ersetzt

questions.explanation: Die moderne integrierte Diagnose verbindet histologische Merkmale mit molekularen Befunden. Der IDH-Status ist zentral für die Abgrenzung wichtiger Entitäten adulter diffuser Gliome. Diagnostik und Terminologie sollten der aktuellen WHO-Klassifikation und der lokalen neuropathologischen Praxis folgen.

distractors.A: Ein MRT kann keine integrierte molekulare Diagnose sichern; sofern klinisch indiziert, sind Gewebegewinnung und molekulare Diagnostik erforderlich.
distractors.C: IDH-mutiertes Astrozytom und Oligodendrogliom sind unterschiedliche Entitäten; eine IDH-Mutation bedeutet nicht automatisch Glioblastom.
distractors.D: Die MGMT-Promotor-Methylierung ist insbesondere als prädiktiver Biomarker relevant, definiert aber nicht allein den integrierten Tumortyp.
distractors.E: Die Histologie bleibt wichtig und wird mit den molekularen Daten integriert.

questions.correlation: Die integrierte Diagnose beeinflusst prognostische Gespräche, interdisziplinäre Therapieplanung und die Eignung für klinische Studien.
questions.pearl: Eine radiologische Verdachtsdiagnose ist kein Ersatz für eine integrierte histomolekulare Diagnose.
references: WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Central Nervous System Tumours, 5. Auflage (2021); spätere Aktualisierungen prüfen.

questions.stem: Ein Patient stellt sich mit plötzlich einsetzendem, sofort maximal ausgeprägtem starken Kopfschmerz vor. Das native kraniale CT ist unauffällig, der klinische Verdacht auf eine aneurysmatische Subarachnoidalblutung bleibt jedoch bestehen. Welches allgemeine Vorgehen ist am sichersten?

options.A: Entlassung, da ein negatives CT eine Blutung unabhängig vom Untersuchungszeitpunkt ausschließt
options.B: Zeit- und leitliniengerechte weiterführende Diagnostik nach lokalem Algorithmus und fachärztlicher Beurteilung
options.C: Beginn einer Antikoagulation bis zur ambulanten Bildgebung
options.D: Bei jedem Patienten ohne Berücksichtigung von Zeitpunkt oder Kontraindikationen eine Lumbalpunktion durchführen
options.E: Bei unauffälligem neurologischem Status von einer Migräne ausgehen

questions.explanation: Die Sensitivität des nativen CT für subarachnoidales Blut hängt unter anderem vom Zeitabstand zum Symptombeginn, der Scannerqualität und der Befundung ab. Bei fortbestehendem Verdacht kann entsprechend einem validierten lokalen Algorithmus, den individuellen Patientenfaktoren und fachärztlicher Einschätzung weitere Diagnostik erforderlich sein.

distractors.A: Ein negatives CT schließt eine SAB nicht in jedem Fall aus; die diagnostische Aussagekraft ist zeitabhängig.
distractors.C: Eine empirische Antikoagulation kann bei einer bestehenden Blutung schädlich sein.
distractors.D: Eine Lumbalpunktion ist nicht bei jedem Patienten automatisch erforderlich; Zeitpunkt, Kontraindikationen und alternative Bildgebungswege sind zu berücksichtigen.
distractors.E: Ein unauffälliger neurologischer Untersuchungsbefund schließt eine SAB nicht zuverlässig aus.

questions.correlation: Der diagnostische Pfad beeinflusst die weitere Entscheidung über Gefäßbildgebung, neurointensivmedizinische Versorgung und Aneurysmatherapie.
questions.pearl: Bei Donnerschlagkopfschmerz den exakten Symptombeginn dokumentieren und den lokal freigegebenen SAB-Algorithmus befolgen. Ein einzelner negativer Test darf nicht außerhalb seines validierten Kontextes interpretiert werden.
references: AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (2023); lokale SOP hat Vorrang.

questions.stem: Welches neu aufgetretene Symptom bei akuten lumbalen radikulären Schmerzen sollte besonders an ein Cauda-equina-Syndrom denken lassen und eine dringliche Abklärung auslösen?

options.C: Neu aufgetretener Harnverhalt oder verändertes Gefühl der Blasenfüllung
options.E: Chronischer axialer Rückenschmerz ohne neurologische Veränderung

questions.explanation: Neu aufgetretener Harnverhalt, veränderte Blasensensibilität, Taubheitsgefühl im Sattelbereich sowie Darm- oder Sexualfunktionsstörungen sind wichtige Warnzeichen eines Cauda-equina-Syndroms. Klinische Beurteilung und dringliche Bildgebung richten sich nach den lokalen Notfallpfaden.

distractors.A: Eine Schmerzverstärkung beim Husten kann bei einer Nervenwurzelreizung auftreten, ist für sich allein jedoch nicht das stärkste Notfallwarnzeichen unter den genannten Optionen.
distractors.B: Einseitige sensible Symptome können bei einer Radikulopathie vorkommen und müssen eingeordnet werden; neu aufgetretene Sphinkterstörungen sind jedoch dringlicher.
distractors.D: Lageabhängige Schmerzen sind häufig und stellen nicht das entscheidende Warnzeichen dar.
distractors.E: Chronischer stabiler axialer Schmerz ohne neue neurologische Symptome spricht weniger für ein akutes Cauda-equina-Syndrom.

questions.correlation: Gezielt nach Blasensensibilität, Miktionsbeginn, Harnstrahl, Sattelsensibilität, Darmfunktion und Sexualfunktion fragen.
questions.pearl: Ein einzelnes Symptom oder eine unauffällige digital-rektale Untersuchung schließt ein Cauda-equina-Syndrom nicht sicher aus. Gesamtkonstellation und dringlichen lokalen Abklärungspfad berücksichtigen.
references: NICE NG59, Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s; lokalen Notfallpfad für Cauda-equina-Syndrom beachten.

questions.stem: Welches Prinzip ist bei der Erstversorgung eines Patienten mit schwerem Schädel-Hirn-Trauma besonders wichtig?

options.A: Eine ausführliche neurologische Untersuchung hat Vorrang vor Atemwegssicherung und Oxygenierung
options.B: Sekundäre Hirnschädigung durch systematische Sicherung von Oxygenierung, Ventilation und Kreislauf verhindern
options.C: HWS-Schutzmaßnahmen beenden, sobald ein kraniales CT angefordert wurde
options.D: Hypotonie als erwünscht ansehen, um den zerebralen Blutfluss zu reduzieren
options.E: Die Behandlung extrakranieller Blutungen bis zur neurochirurgischen Beurteilung zurückstellen

questions.explanation: Die initiale Traumaversorgung folgt strukturierten Reanimations- und Behandlungsprinzipien. Hypoxie und Hypotonie können eine sekundäre Hirnschädigung verstärken. Daher müssen Atemweg, Oxygenierung, Ventilation und Kreislauf frühzeitig adressiert werden, parallel zum Schutz der Halswirbelsäule und zur koordinierten Traumaversorgung.

distractors.A: Lebensbedrohliche physiologische Störungen haben Priorität; die ausführliche neurologische Untersuchung folgt den initialen Stabilisierungsschritten.
distractors.C: HWS-Schutzmaßnahmen bleiben relevant, bis eine Freigabe nach geeignetem Protokoll erfolgt.
distractors.D: Hypotonie gefährdet die zerebrale Perfusion und ist kein therapeutisches Ziel.
distractors.E: Lebensbedrohliche extrakranielle Blutungen müssen im Rahmen der Traumaversorgung unverzüglich behandelt werden.

questions.correlation: Serielle neurologische Kontrollen, Pupillenbefund, GCS-Komponenten und physiologische Parameter helfen, eine Verschlechterung früh zu erkennen.
questions.pearl: Vermeidbare Hypoxie und Hypotonie verhindern. Die einzelnen GCS-Komponenten dokumentieren, nicht nur den Summenwert.
references: NICE NG232, Head injury: assessment and early management (2023); lokales Traumaprotokoll.

questions.stem: Welcher Befund kann bei einem Säugling ein klinischer Hinweis auf einen progredienten Hydrozephalus sein?

options.A: Ein stabiler Kopfumfang entlang der bisherigen Perzentile
options.B: Ein rasch zunehmender Kopfumfang mit Überschreiten von Perzentilenlinien
options.D: Eine bei ruhiger Untersuchung normale, weiche Fontanelle

questions.explanation: Ein rasch zunehmender Kopfumfang, insbesondere mit Überschreiten von Perzentilenlinien, kann bei Säuglingen auf eine progrediente Ventrikelerweiterung hinweisen. Der Befund muss zusammen mit Entwicklungsverlauf, klinischer Untersuchung und geeigneter Bildgebung beurteilt werden.

distractors.A: Ein stabiler Verlauf ist im Allgemeinen weniger auffällig als eine rasche Veränderung, schließt eine Erkrankung aber nicht aus.
distractors.C: Schluckauf ist unspezifisch und weist isoliert nicht auf einen Hydrozephalus hin.
distractors.D: Eine zu einem Untersuchungszeitpunkt weiche Fontanelle schließt einen Hydrozephalus nicht aus.
distractors.E: Ein isolierter Husten ist kein charakteristischer Hinweis auf einen progredienten Hydrozephalus.

questions.correlation: Kopfumfang im Verlauf, Fontanelle, Schädelnähte, Augenbewegungen, Trinkverhalten, Vigilanz und Entwicklung beurteilen.
